entities.summary:
The situation where color is created by mixing the visible light emitted from differently colored light sources

Additive color, also known as RGB color, is a fundamental principle in the production of colors, particularly in digital displays. This phenomenon occurs when red, green, and blue light are combined in various intensities, resulting in a broad spectrum of hues. The additive color mixing model is the foundation for modern digital displays, including televisions, computer monitors, and mobile devices, which utilize combinations of red, green, and blue sub-pixels to produce a wide range of colors.

The discovery of additive color predates modern digital technology, with early experiments in light and color dating back to the early 19th century. One notable figure, James Clerk Maxwell, demonstrated the principles of additive color in the 1860s through a series of experiments using three colored filters and a beam of white light. His work laid the groundwork for the development of modern color theory and the creation of digital displays.

Additive color has far-reaching consequences in various fields, including art, design, and technology. Its widespread adoption has enabled the creation of vibrant and dynamic visual content, from digital art to high-definition video. Furthermore, additive color has paved the way for advancements in color reproduction and display technology, allowing for the development of more accurate and lifelike color representation in modern displays.

The widespread use of additive color has led to a 'color revolution' in modern design and art. As one prominent artist noted, 'The ability to create an infinite range of colors has opened up new possibilities for creativity and self-expression.'
